readme.title: CRLF Injection and HTTP Header Injection

blocks.text: CRLF injection happens when untrusted input containing carriage-return and line-feed characters (`\r\n`, `%0d%0a`) is written into an HTTP response header, a redirect `Location`, a log line, an email header or a raw protocol stream. The attacker can add headers, set cookies, split a response, or inject a body. Many frameworks now reject bare CR/LF in header values, but custom proxies, older stacks, URL parsers and non-HTTP protocols still fail.

items: Reflected parameters in `Location`, `Set-Cookie`, `Content-Disposition` and custom response headers
Header-to-header propagation through proxies and `X-Forwarded-*` handling
Request splitting against HTTP/1.1 clients in SSRF paths (URL host, path or user-info containing CRLF)
Unicode characters that normalise or truncate to CR/LF (`%E5%98%8A%E5%98%8D`)
Email, SMTP, IMAP, Redis and Memcached text protocols reached through SSRF or injection (see `Email-Injection/` and `SSRF/`)

blocks.text: Inject a harmless marker header (`X-Injected: crlf-marker`) and check whether it appears in the response headers or on a downstream hop, not just reflected in the body. Test every encoding the stack might decode once: raw, single URL-encoded, double URL-encoded, and Unicode forms. Inspect the raw response in a proxy; browsers hide split headers. Confirm that a cookie set through injection actually reaches the browser jar before reporting session fixation. For response splitting, verify against a fixture because modern servers normally block it.
See `crlf-injection-payloads.txt`. Each line is an independent value to place in a parameter, path segment or header. Replace `app.example.test` with a controlled host.

sections.label: Unicode and overlong forms that some stacks collapse to CR/LF
Cookie injection (session fixation test: use a throwaway cookie name)
Response splitting: terminate headers and inject a body (works only on stacks that do not validate header values)
Security header suppression and cache poisoning probes
Path-based injection (CRLF in URL path reflected in header)
Request header injection reaching an upstream (put in a header value that the proxy forwards)
SSRF request splitting through the URL host, user-info or path (target fetches the URL with HTTP/1.1)
Text protocol smuggling reached through SSRF or URL fetchers (raw commands in a URL path)
HTTP/2 downgrade variants (header values with CRLF sent in HTTP/2, which the front end must reject)
